Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis.   • Hepatic adenoma: hemorrhage is a common feature; arterial hyperenhancement, fat, multiplicity, encapsulation/pseudocapsule, and hemorrhagic heterogeneity may support the diagnosis.
  • HCC: intratumoral spontaneous hemorrhage is uncommon, but large HCC can rupture through the capsule; arterial hyperenhancement, portal/delayed washout, capsule, and cirrhotic background are key pivots.
  • Hemorrhagic hepatic cyst: clot may mimic a solid tumor, but blood products do not enhance; ultrasound may show organizing hematoma/fibrin strands and MRI signal depends on the blood stage.
  • ADPLD: innumerable nonenhancing simple cysts may be present; on T1 MRI, simple-fluid cysts are dark while hemorrhagic cysts can be bright.
  • Coagulopathic hemorrhage: look for a hematocrit level, active bleeding, and bleeding at multiple sites; hepatic defects may mimic traumatic lacerations.

  • Less common: coagulopathic hepatic hemorrhage, hepatic metastases, HELLP syndrome, and amyloidosis.
🧪 Modality Pivots
  • Core HCC: classic CT/MRI pattern is arterial enhancement with portal venous washout and an enhancing capsule; HCC can be slightly T2 hyperintense and may restrict diffusion.
  • Core adenoma: arterial hyperenhancement with iso- or hypoenhancement on portal venous/delayed phases; ultrasound appearance is variable; sulfur-colloid uptake is usually reduced; Core describes typically little HIDA uptake. IDA uptake occurs in hepatocytes, so absent ductules should not be equated with absent initial hepatocyte uptake.

  • Do not universalize attenuation: the article gives >60 HU as a possible NECT appearance of blood, while a melanoma case had 35-HU hemoperitoneum.

  • Case-specific embolization or medication-withdrawal outcomes are examples, not universal treatment algorithms.

Hemorrhage in or around a focal hepatic lesion can reflect trauma, benign or malignant tumor, cystic disease, coagulopathy, metastasis, or pregnancy-related liver injury. Recognition depends on identifying blood, the lesion substrate, the enhancement pattern, and whether bleeding is intratumoral, subcapsular, or intraperitoneal.

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis. Core Radiology liver coverage was reviewed for HCC, adenoma, cystic liver disease, metastases, and liver trauma; RadPrimer supplies the differential hierarchy and shared article backbone; STATdx supplies the selected 23-image teaching library and additional case detail.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings
  • Hemorrhage may be heterogeneous high attenuation >60 HU on NECT or appear as high-intensity foci on T1WI and T2WI; bleeding may extend subcapsularly or intraperitoneally.
  • Hepatic trauma: lacerations are usually linear or stellate; dual-phase CT is the preferred tool in hemodynamically stable patients.
  • Hepatic adenoma: hemorrhage is a common feature; arterial hyperenhancement, fat, multiplicity, encapsulation/pseudocapsule, and hemorrhagic heterogeneity may support the diagnosis.
  • HCC: intratumoral spontaneous hemorrhage is uncommon, but large HCC can rupture through the capsule; arterial hyperenhancement, portal/delayed washout, capsule, and cirrhotic background are key pivots.
  • Hemorrhagic hepatic cyst: clot may mimic a solid tumor, but blood products do not enhance; ultrasound may show organizing hematoma/fibrin strands and MRI signal depends on the blood stage.
  • ADPLD: innumerable nonenhancing simple cysts may be present; on T1 MRI, simple-fluid cysts are dark while hemorrhagic cysts can be bright.
  • Coagulopathic hemorrhage: look for a hematocrit level, active bleeding, and bleeding at multiple sites; hepatic defects may mimic traumatic lacerations.
  • Hemorrhagic metastases are uncommon and are usually associated with hypervascular metastases; article examples include pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor and melanoma.
  • HELLP can produce intrahepatic or subcapsular hematoma, active extravasation, and wedge-shaped hepatic infarcts.
⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Common: hepatic trauma, hepatic adenoma, HCC, hepatic cyst, and autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease.
  • Less common: coagulopathic hepatic hemorrhage, hepatic metastases, HELLP syndrome, and amyloidosis.
🧪 Modality Pivots
  • Core HCC: classic CT/MRI pattern is arterial enhancement with portal venous washout and an enhancing capsule; HCC can be slightly T2 hyperintense and may restrict diffusion.
  • Core adenoma: arterial hyperenhancement with iso- or hypoenhancement on portal venous/delayed phases; ultrasound appearance is variable; sulfur-colloid uptake is usually reduced; Core describes typically little HIDA uptake. IDA uptake occurs in hepatocytes, so absent ductules should not be equated with absent initial hepatocyte uptake.
  • Core simple cyst: anechoic with posterior enhancement and no Doppler flow on US; 0-20 HU and nonenhancing on CT; low T1/high T2 and nonenhancing on MRI.
  • Core metastases: most are hypovascular and best seen on portal venous CT; metastases are usually T1 hypointense/T2 hyperintense, while blood products or melanin may be T1 hyperintense; ultrasound may show a target sign.
⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • Do not universalize attenuation: the article gives >60 HU as a possible NECT appearance of blood, while a melanoma case had 35-HU hemoperitoneum.
  • Do not equate T1 hyperintensity with fat. The source captions attribute the adenoma foci to hemorrhage, but their referenced T2 images are not staged. Intracellular lipid is assessed by opposed-phase signal loss; T2 brightness alone is not a definitive blood-versus-fat test.
  • A sentinel clot immediately adjacent to a lesion localizes the likely bleeding source.
  • Case-specific embolization or medication-withdrawal outcomes are examples, not universal treatment algorithms.
⭐ Super Summary
  • First prove blood, then identify the substrate: trauma, adenoma, HCC, cystic disease, coagulopathy, metastasis, or HELLP.
  • Enhancement is a major separator: nonenhancing clot within a cyst differs from a vascular tumor; arterialized masses require adenoma/HCC/metastatic considerations.
  • Report active bleeding, subcapsular/intraperitoneal extension, infarction, and tumor-in-vein when present because these findings change urgency or management.
